title: A healthy cell can be read against itself: the first steps to an instrument that needs no reference library (in progress)
set_out: Goal for the day: an instrument built from physics alone, so a sample can be read without a library of other people's cells (an atlas) and without lab-by-lab calibration. Every test ran on made-up data first, then on real data once.

sections.heading: What ran, and how each came out
sections.lead: Each prediction was written down before its data was read, and every counting method was first checked on made-up data with a known answer.

entries.title: Every healthy cell follows the same simple rule
entries.what: Cells tag their DNA to remember what kind of cell they are, and make a few tagging mistakes. Across 56 kinds of healthy human cells, the number of mistakes depends on one thing: how much of its DNA the cell keeps loosely tagged. All 56 fall on one straight line (53 within 0.003 of it). Whiteboard part 7 (the loose end read off the line); made reproducible as committed scripts with manifest rows PHY-045 and PHY-046.
entries.why: This is what lets an instrument know what a healthy cell should look like from that cell's own sample, instead of looking it up in an atlas. It is the central step toward a test that does not depend on any one lab's reference data.

entries.title: The rule holds with a cut set by physics
entries.what: The line first used a borrowed cut (70 percent tagged) to call a stretch of DNA loose. Replaced with the physics value, 2/3, where a stretch is held by at least one bit's worth of energy: the line holds (r 0.85) and the cells keep the same order (0.996 agreement). Box job eef8d756, manifest PHY-048.
entries.why: The result does not hinge on a number someone chose; it comes from the physics.

entries.title: The rule from each sample's own DNA pieces, with no arrays
entries.what: Read straight from each sample's own sequenced pieces of DNA, with nothing borrowed from other data, the same line comes back (r 0.81; odds of chance about 1 in 10 trillion). It is weaker and the firm rate moved, and young progenitor cells sit below it, and the whole-genome version (box job 2d3d817b) gave the same picture: r 0.79, the same firm rate, on all 56 cells once ten refused downloads were re-read. Manifest PHY-049.
entries.why: The first reading of the gauge with no atlas and no arrays at all.

entries.title: Island side with the eraser removed: read once
entries.what: The DNA's bare 'islands' are kept clean 1.7 times better than the writer enzyme alone allows. Removing the eraser enzyme barely changed that (1.07 times), so a shield, not the eraser, keeps them clean. Manifest PHY-046.
entries.why: Narrows what holds a cell's identity in place, the next piece to derive.

entries.title: Tumors: both sides of the DNA now being read
entries.what: DEV-BACKBONE-01 island side approved; the island arm added and its synthetic run (planted changes read correctly in all six pairs); island arm real counts submitted on the second machine: six early-onset colorectal cancer patients, tumor and normal tissue, re-read on both sides. Manifest PHY-043.
entries.why: The first test of the new rule on cancer: does a tumor read off its own line?

entries.title: The horizon's storage by era
entries.what: The cosmic horizon held 6e113 bits when the CMB was released and holds 3.3e122 today; half of today's total was written after the expansion began to speed up. Manifest PHY-053.
entries.why: A number-by-number history for the Computer Science of Reality paper.

entries.title: Second-laboratory candidates found (metadata only, PHY-047)
entries.what: Another lab's sorted immune cells (ENCODE) for development, and two sets of sorted healthy T cells nobody has opened yet, kept for the final sealed test. No data read.
entries.why: The rule must hold in a second lab before anyone should trust it.

entries.title: Atlas v2.1: the fit is running and healthy
entries.what: 164 of 700 blocks done by 7:45 AM Pacific, about 20 blocks an hour. No divergent draws in any block; in every block, 99 percent of sites show an R-hat of 1.009 or less. Watchers on both machines check every 10 minutes for a stalled or idle box.
entries.why: The fit is the map every other instrument reads against. Expected to finish Friday October 16, about 9 AM Pacific.

entries.title: Sealed before the atlas exists: the Loyfer and Moss use tests
entries.what: Two jobs a reference atlas is built for: finding each cell's marker sites, and working out which cells are in a mixed sample. Atlas v2.1 is compared with Moss's published reference on the same held-out arrays, including mixtures with brain and lung cells Moss's reference does not hold. Each bar was first checked on made-up data to pass when it should and fail when it should; the first version of one bar could not see a planted worse atlas and was fixed before any real data. At the author's direction the bars are a showcase, not a referee's gate.
entries.why: So the atlas is judged on the job its users actually need, by rules fixed before its first value exists.

sections.heading: What we learned that we did not know yesterday

entries.title: A healthy cell carries its own reference
entries.what: Its expected tagging mistakes follow from how loosely it holds its DNA, one straight line for every cell type tested.
entries.why: The reason a future test may need no library of other people's cells.

entries.title: One loose level for every kind of cell
entries.what: Loosely held DNA makes the same rate of mistakes in every cell type.

entries.title: The cell's bare islands are held by a shield, not the eraser
entries.what: Bare islands hold at 4.38 kT against 3.83 kT for the firm tags.

entries.title: What the new instrument can read
entries.what: Any organism that tags its DNA, from any lab, wherever single-piece sequencing exists: public nanopore genomes, plants grown at two temperatures, dogs, unread salmon data (PHY-058 to PHY-068).
entries.why: Opens far more data than the old reference-bound instrument could use.

entries.what: Two running tests, several planned ones and the plain-language series were missing from the Master Testing Manifest, and the atlas fit still read 'planned'.

entries.title: Front page: the loose-end line as an early result (author approved the wording)

entries.title: A plain-language series and a grand final test
entries.what: An eight-part plain-language series (OTH-041 to OTH-048), and one sealed test on fresh data to commission the instrument (COM-IAMA-052).

entries.title: A commissioning plan for every instrument (author)
entries.what: Twenty-one steps in four stages: tonight's work; scoring the atlas when it lands; commissioning IAM-A without an atlas, ending in one grand sealed test on fresh data; then the C-Score, Met-A cell by cell, Group-A, whole blood and plasma. Two new manifest rows: a database of every instrument's readings (OTH-051), and the concern line, where a reading first leaves the healthy line before it reaches tumor territory (PHY-069). Only three derivations stay on the near list, because they improve accuracy now; the rest wait until the catalogue is commissioned.
entries.why: So the work runs in order without being pulled sideways.

entries.title: The front README made short; the long sections moved to REFERENCE.md (author)
entries.what: The README now points to the page, the daily logs, the instrument catalogue, the manifest and the book; its live parts are generated from the same files as the page.
entries.why: So the most current work is what a visitor sees first.
